ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 32 (Miller 1851 / Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 28, which numbers Book X 1-30)
greek: Θεὸς εἷς ὁ πρῶτος καὶ μόνος καὶ ἀπάντων ποιητὴς καὶ κύριος, σύγχρονον ἔσχεν οὐδέν, οὐ χάος ἄπειρον, οὐχ ὕδωρ ἀμέτρητον ἢ γῆν στερρὰν, οὐχὶ ἀέρα πυκνόν, οὐ πῦρ θερμὸν, οὐ πνεῦμα λεπτὸν, οὐκ οὐρανοῦ μεγάλου κυανέαν μορφήν· ἀλλ' ἦν εἷς μόνος ἑαυτῷ, ὃς θελήσας ἐποίησε τὰ ὄντα οὐκ ὄντα πρότερον, πλὴν ὅτε ἠθέλησε ποιεῖν ὡς ἔμπειρος ὢν τῶν ἐσομένων.

Greek 10.32 opening (Miller p.334, lines 1-7 of the page image).
english: The first and only (one God), both Creator and Lord of all, had nothing coeval with Himself; not infinite chaos, nor measureless water, nor solid earth, nor dense air, not warm fire, nor refined spirit, nor the azure canopy  of the stupendous firmament. But He was One, alone in Himself. By an exercise of His will He created things that are, which antecedently had no existence, except that He willed to make them. For He is fully acquainted with whatever is about to take place.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 334 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 150
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: God is the one first and only principle, Creator and Lord of all, with nothing coeval to Him; he is 'alone in himself' before creating.
limits: Weak support: the passage speaks of God before creation and says nothing about the Logos or the Spirit here. 'Alone in himself' is the Unitarian/monarchian-sounding phrase opponents cite; the Nicene reply reads it as the unbegotten principle prior to the Logos, which the next chapters make explicit. Not checked: scholarly assessments (Kelly, Hanson, Simonetti) are not verified in this run.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29 first paragraph)
greek: Οὗτος οὖν μόνος καὶ κατὰ πάντων Θεὸς, λόγον πρῶτον ἐννοηθεὶς ἀπογεννᾷ, οὐ λόγον ὡς φωνὴν, ἀλλ' ἐνδιάθετον τοῦ παντὸς λογισμόν. Τοῦτον μόνον ἐξ ὄντων ἐγέννα· τὸ γὰρ ὄν, αὐτὸς ὁ πατὴρ ἦν, ἐξ οὗ τὸ γεννηθῆναι αἴτιον τοῖς γινομένοις.
greek_edition: Miller, Origenis Philosophumena sive Omnium Haeresium Refutatio (Oxford: Typ. Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Greek 10.33 opening, Miller pp.334-335.
english: Therefore this solitary and supreme Deity, by an exercise of reflection, brought forth the Logos first; not the word in the sense of being articulated by voice, but as a ratiocination of the universe, conceived and residing in the divine mind. Him alone He produced from existing things; for the Father Himself constituted existence, and the being born from Him was the cause of all things that are produced.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 334-335 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 150
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: God the Father, reasoning, first brings forth the Logos as a thought conceived in the divine mind, not as an articulated word; 'from existing things' ('ἐξ ὄντων') is the phrase of production.
limits: Key distinction is between the Logos 'endiathetos' (inner reason) and the spoken word; this is the prolation/generation scheme of Hippolytus, not a statement of eternal begetting. 'ἐξ ὄντων ἐγέννα' ('begat from existing things') is the hard phrase: Arians read it as production from being, and the 'Father Himself was being' clause is the reply. Greek line break 'ἐξ ὄν-' (p.334) continues on p.335.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: Λόγος ἦν ἐν αὐτῷ φέρων τὸ θέλειν τοῦ γεγεννηκότος, οὐκ ἄπειρος τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς ἐννοίας· ἅμα γὰρ τῷ ἐκ τοῦ γεννήσαντος προελθεῖν πρωτότοκος τούτου γενόμενος, φωνὴν ἔχει ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὰς ἐν τῷ πατρικῷ ἐννοηθείσας ἰδέας, ὅθεν κελεύοντος πατρὸς γίνεσθαι κόσμον τὸ κατὰ ἓν Λόγος ἀπετελεῖτο ἀρέσκων Θεῷ.
greek_edition: Miller, Origenis Philosophumena sive Omnium Haeresium Refutatio (Oxford: Typ. Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller p.335, opening of the Logos paragraph.
english: The Logos was in the Father Himself, bearing the will of His progenitor, and not being unacquainted with the mind of the Father. For simultaneously  with His procession from His Progenitor, inasmuch as He is this Progenitor's first-born, He has, as a voice in Himself, the ideas conceived in the Father. And so it was, that when the Father ordered the world to come into existence, the Logos one by one completed each object of creation, thus pleasing God.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 335 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 150
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: The Logos is in the Father, knows his mind, and at the same moment as proceeding from him is the firstborn, holding the Father's ideas as a voice in himself; he executes the creation the Father orders.
limits: Shows the Logos as Son/firstborn and as distinct in act from the Father, but the time relation is stated as 'simultaneously' (ἅμα) with the procession, which the subordinationist reads as a temporal sequence in God; 'προελθεῖν' (procession) is the same verb as the Logos-as-emission scheme. The Logos is also 'serving' the Father's order (see item 04 on ὑπουργῇ).

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: Καὶ γὰρ αἱ τούτων πρῶται οὐσίαι ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων γενόμεναι, πῦρ καὶ πνεῦμα, ὕδωρ καὶ γῆ, οὔτε ἄρσενα οὔτε θήλεα ὑπάρχειν ἑκάστῃ τούτων δύνανται προελθεῖν ἄρσενα καὶ θήλεα, πλὴν εἰ βούλοιτο ὁ κελεύων Θεὸς ἵνα Λόγος ὑπουργῇ.

Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller p.335, the middle of the cosmogony paragraph.
english: For even the primary substances of these, which were formed out of nonentities, viz., fire and spirit, water and earth, are neither male nor female; nor could male or female proceed from any one of these, were it not that God, who is the source of all authority, wished that the Logos might render assistance  in accomplishing a production of this kind.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 335 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 151
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: The primary elements are neither male nor female unless God, who commands, wishes that the Logos should 'serve' (ὑπουργεῖν) in producing them.
limits: Objection: the Logos is said to 'render assistance' (ὑπουργῇ) to God's command, the vocabulary of a servant/minister, which Arians and Unitarians cite for a subordinate Logos. The context is cosmogony of sexes and elements, not the Logos's nature; no answer is given in the text beyond the general 'Logos executes what the Father orders'.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: Ταῦτα λόγῳ ἐδημιούργει, ἑτέρως γενέσθαι μὴ δυνάμενα, ἢ ὡς ἐγένετο. Ὅτε δὲ (ἡ) ὡς ἠθέλησε καὶ ἐποίησεν, ὀνόματι καλέσας ἐσήμηνεν.
greek_edition: Miller, Origenis Philosophumena sive Omnium Haeresium Refutatio (Oxford: Typ. Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller p.335, lines 11-16.
english: These things He created through the Logos, it not being possible for things to be generated otherwise than as they were produced. But when, according as He willed, He also formed (objects), He called them by names, and thus notified His creative effort.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 335 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 151
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: God creates these things 'through the Logos' ('λόγῳ'), and when he wills and makes, he names them.
limits: 'Through the Logos' (λόγῳ) can be read instrumentally (Logos as tool, as in Arian 'organ' readings) and the 'when He willed' clause is cited for a Logos that is temporally subject to the will. The ANF translation says 'through the Logos'; the Greek 'λόγῳ' is ambiguous between 'through the Word' and 'by the word (command)'. Hippolytus's own ch. 29 says the Logos 'completed each object', so agency is not denied. Greek word 'Ὅτε δὲ (ἡ)' has a bracketed 'ἡ' in Miller's text (not a real-word reading).

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: οὐ θεὸν θέλων ποιεῖν ἔσφηλεν, οὐδὲ ἄγγελον (μὴ πλανῶ), ἀλλ' ἄνθρωπον. Εἰ γὰρ θεόν σε ἠθέλησε ποιῆσαι, ἐδύνατο· ἔχεις τοῦ Λόγου τὸ παράδειγμα· ἄνθρωπον θέλων, ἄνθρωπόν σε ἐποίησεν.

Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller pp.335-336 (ἔσφηλεν begins p.336).
english: The Creator did not wish to make him a god, and failed in His aim; nor an angel — be not deceived, — but a man. For if He had willed to make you a god, He could have done so. You have the example of the Logos. His will, however, was, that you should be a man, and He has made you a man.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 335-336 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 151
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: Man is made a man, not a god or an angel, because that was God's will; God could have made him a god had he willed, and the Logos is the example.
limits: The Logos is cited as an 'example' (παράδειγμα) of what God wills for man. Opponents (Unitarians and Muslim polemic) use the phrase to argue that the Logos is a created model; the passage itself does not say the Logos is a man or a creature. The line 'He could have made you a god' is about the creator's power over human nature, not about the Logos's ousia.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: εἰ δὲ θέλεις καὶ θεὸς γενέσθαι, ὑπάκουε τῷ πεποιηκότι, καὶ μὴ ἀντίβαινε νῦν, ἵνα ἐπὶ τῷ μικρῷ πιστὸς εὑρεθεὶς, καὶ τὸ μέγα πιστευθῆναι δυνηθῇς.
greek_edition: Miller, Origenis Philosophumena sive Omnium Haeresium Refutatio (Oxford: Typ. Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller p.336, line 22-26 of the page image.
english: But if you are desirous of also becoming a god, obey Him that has created you, and resist not now, in order that, being found faithful in that which is small, you may be enabled to have entrusted to you also that which is great.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 336 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 151
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: If you want to become a god, obey the Creator now, so that being faithful in small things you may be entrusted with great things.
limits: The 'becoming god' is conditional on obedience and is a human destiny ('καὶ θεὸς γενέσθαι'), not a claim that the Logos is one 'god' in the way a man can be. Unitarian and Muslim critics cite deification language as incompatible with the uniqueness of God; the reply is that Hippolytus speaks of a gift/destiny, not of a nature. Not verified here: whether the Greek 'γενέσθαι' is in some codices read differently (Miller's apparatus not checked for this line).

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: Τούτου ὁ Λόγος μόνος ἐξ αὐτοῦ· διὸ καὶ θεὸς, οὐσία ὑπάρχων Θεοῦ. Ὁ δὲ κόσμος ἐξ οὐδενός· διὸ οὐ θεός· οὗτος ἐπιδέχεται καὶ λύσιν ὅτε βούλεται ὁ κτίσας.
greek_edition: Miller, Origenis Philosophumena sive Omnium Haeresium Refutatio (Oxford: Typ. Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller p.336, line 22-23 (the phrase is on the page image, 'Τούτου ὁ Λόγος μόνος ἐξ αὐτοῦ').
english: The Logos alone of this God is from God himself; wherefore also the Logos is God, being the substance of God. Now the world was made from nothing; wherefore it is not God; as also because this world admits of dissolution whenever the Creator so wishes it.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 336 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 151
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: The Logos alone is from God himself, so he is God, being the substance (ousia) of God; the world is from nothing, so it is not God and can be dissolved at the Creator's will.
limits: The strongest Trinitarian-looking sentence in the chapter: 'the Logos is God' and 'being the ousia of God'. Two Arian counters apply: (a) 'θεὸς' is anarthrous (no article), which can read as 'a god / divine' rather than 'God'; (b) 'ἐξ αὐτοῦ' ('from Himself') can be read as origin from the Father without equal essence. Whether 'οὐσία' here means 'substance' in the Nicene sense is contested; not verified in this run. Scholarly defences (Bull, Newman) and critics (Kelly, Hanson) are NOT checked in this run.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: Ἔγγιον ἡμῶν διὰ τοῦ προειρημένου Μωϋσέως, ἀνδρὸς εὐλαβοῦς καὶ θεοφιλοῦς, νόμος ὡρίζετο πλήρης σεμνότητος καὶ δικαιοσύνης. Τὰ δὲ πάντα διοικεῖ ὁ Λόγος ὁ Θεοῦ, ὁ πρωτόγονος πατρὸς παῖς, ἢ πρὸ ἑωσφόρου φωσφόρος φωνή·
greek_edition: Miller, Origenis Philosophumena sive Omnium Haeresium Refutatio (Oxford: Typ. Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller p.336, line 43-44.
english: Nearer our own day was there established a law, full of gravity and justice, by Moses, to whom allusion has been already made, a devout man, and one beloved of God. Now the Logos of God controls all these; the first begotten Child of the Father, the voice of the Dawn antecedent to the Morning Star.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 336 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 151
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: The Logos of God governs all things; he is the firstborn child of the Father, a voice (phōnē) shining before the morning star.
limits: 'Πατρὸς παῖς' (child of the Father) and 'ὁ Λόγος ὁ Θεοῦ' support a filial Logos. But 'πρωτόγονος' (firstborn) is the word Arians use for a created first being (cf. Col 1:15), and 'φωνή' (voice) can be read as impersonal speech. Hippolytus's own 'the Logos is God' (item 08) is the counter-reading. Not checked: whether Hippolytus here uses 'παῖς' as 'Son' or 'child'.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 33 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 29)
greek: Τοῦτον τὸν Λόγον ἐν ὑστέροις ἀπέστελλεν ὁ πατὴρ οὐκέτι διὰ προφήτου λαλεῖν, οὐ σκοτεινῶς κηρυσσόμενον ὑπονοεῖσθαι θέλων, ἀλλ' αὐτοψεὶ φανερωθῆναι τοῦτον λέγων,
greek_edition: Miller, Origenis Philosophumena sive Omnium Haeresium Refutatio (Oxford: Typ. Acad., 1851), read by eye from the page images of archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp (PDF pp. 352-357 = printed pp. 334-339) at 200 dpi; NOT machine OCR (the djvu text layer has no usable Greek). Accents and breathings read from the image; not collated against Wendland GCS 26 or Marcovich 1986. Scan: https://archive.org/details/origenisphilosop00hipp . Miller p.337, lines 1-3.
english: This Logos the Father in the latter days sent forth, no longer to speak by a prophet, and not wishing that the Word, being obscurely proclaimed, should be made the subject of mere conjecture, but that He should be manifested, so that we could see Him with our own eyes.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 337 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 152
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: In the last days the Father sent this Logos, not to speak through a prophet, but to be seen in person.
limits: Mission language ('the Father sent forth') is the classic subordinationist argument (sent one is less than the sender). Hippolytus uses it of the incarnate manifestation. The same chapter (Greek 10.33, ANF 29-30) says the Logos took a body from a virgin, which supports a personal Logos distinct from the Father, but it does not state eternal coequality. Not checked: the Greek 'ἀπέστελλεν' in other MSS (Miller apparatus).

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 34 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 30, 'The Author's Concluding Address')
greek: Τοιοῦτος ὁ περὶ τὸ Θεῖον ἀληθὴς λόγος, ὦ ἄνθρωποι Ἕλληνές τε καὶ βάρβαροι, Χαλδαῖοί τε καὶ Ἀσσύριοι, Αἰγύπτιοί τε καὶ Λίβυες, Ἰνδοί τε καὶ Αἰθίοπες, Κελτοί τε καὶ οἱ στρατηγοῦντες Λατῖνοι, πάντες τε οἱ τὴν Εὐρώπην Ἀσίαν τε καὶ Λιβύην κατοικοῦντες, οἷς σύμβουλος ἐγὼ γίνομαι, φιλανθρώπου Λόγου ὑπάρχων μαθητὴς καὶ φιλάνθρωπος, ὅπως προσδραμόντες διδαχθῆτε παρ' ἡμῶν τίς ὁ ὄντως Θεὸς καὶ ἡ τούτου εὔτακτος δημιουργία

english: Such is the true doctrine in regard of the divine nature, O you men, Greeks and Barbarians, Chaldeans and Assyrians, Egyptians and Libyans, Indians and Ethiopians, Celts, and you Latins, who lead armies, and all you that inhabit Europe, and Asia, and Libya.  And to you I have become an adviser, inasmuch as I am a disciple of the benevolent Logos, and hence humane, in order that you may hasten and by us may be taught who the true God is, and what is His well-ordered creation.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 338 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 152
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: Hippolytus presents this as the true doctrine of the divine nature, taught from the Logos, for all peoples, so that they learn who the true God is.
limits: Context only: it states the author's claim to teach 'who the true God is' through the Logos; it does not define the Trinity. Note that the ANF/MacMahon English 'who the true God is' is in the Greek 'τίς ὁ ὄντως Θεὸς', so the author's own claim is to teach the true God, not a triad formula.

ref: Refutatio omnium haeresium, Book X, ch. 34 (Miller/Greek numbering; = ANF vol. 5 Book X ch. 30)
greek: Γέγονας γὰρ θεός· ὅσα γὰρ ὑπέμεινας πάθῃ ἄνθρωπος ὢν, ταῦτα δίδου ὅτι ἄνθρωπος εἶς· ὅσα δὲ παρακολουθεῖ θεῷ, ταῦτα παρέχειν ἐπήγγελαι Θεὸς, ὅτε θεοποιηθῇς, ἀθάνατος γεννηθείς.

english: For you have become God:  for whatever sufferings you underwent while being a man, these He gave to you, because you were of mortal mould, but whatever it is consistent with God to impart, these God has promised to bestow upon you, because you have been deified, and begotten unto immortality.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 339 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 153
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: 'You have become god': sufferings that a man undergoes are given because he is mortal, but what belongs to God is promised, because you have been deified and begotten immortal.
limits: The clearest 'deification' text in the set: 'γέγονας θεός' ('you have become god') and 'θεοποιηθῇς' ('when you are deified'). Unitarian and Muslim critics cite it as a claim that man can be god; the text itself places the divinising as a future/eschatological gift ('ὅτε θεοποιηθῇς', 'when you are deified') and the Greek 'γέγονας' is in context of promised immortality. MacMahon's 'these He gave to you' does not clearly match Miller's printed 'ταῦτα δίδου' (the form is ambiguous; not resolved). Not checked: how Nicene writers used 'θεοποίησις'.

english: Be not therefore inflamed, O you men, with enmity one towards another, nor hesitate to retrace  with all speed your steps. For Christ is the God above all, and He has arranged to wash away sin from human beings, rendering regenerate the old man.
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 339 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 153
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: Christ is the God over all, who has arranged to wash away human sin and make the old man new.
limits: Direct statement that Christ is 'God over all' (κατὰ πάντων Θεός). Two limits: the phrase 'God over all' is used of the Father in some NT and patristic contexts (e.g. Eph 4:6), so its application here must be read in context; and the Greek is 'Θεός' with article-less predicate (no article), which the Arian reads as a predicate 'a god'. ANF renders 'the God above all'. The text does not discuss a Spirit.

greek: οὗ προστάγμασιν ὑπακούσας σεμνοῖς, καὶ ἀγαθοῦ ἀγαθὸς γενόμενος μιμητὴς, ἔσῃ ὅμοιος ὑπ' αὐτοῦ τιμηθείς. Σοῦ γὰρ πτωχεύει Θεὸς καὶ σὲ θεὸν ποιήσας εἰς δόξαν αὐτοῦ.

english: And provided you obey His solemn injunctions, and becomest a faithful follower of Him who is good, you shall resemble Him, inasmuch as you shall have honour conferred upon you by Him. For the Deity, (by condescension,) does not diminish anything of the divinity of His divine  perfection; having made you even God unto His glory!
translator: J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5, 1886); text as transcribed on New Advent, which is revised and modernizes some pronouns (1919 Scribner scan reads 'ye/thou' in places)
page: Miller 1851 printed p. 339 (Greek); ANF vol. 5, ANF 5 page per 1919 Scribner reprint scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather05robe), estimated from OCR page headers, +/-1: 153
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, transl. J. H. MacMahon (Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1886), as transcribed on New Advent (revised by K. Knight) ; Greek: Miller, Oxford 1851
what_it_says: By obeying God's solemn commands you will resemble him and be honoured by him; God 'becomes poor' for you and makes you God for his glory.
limits: The Greek verb 'πτωχεύει' means 'becomes poor' (a kenotic image), but MacMahon renders it 'does not diminish ... (by condescension)' which is an interpretive gloss; a reader of the Greek will see a kenosis-language that Arians could cite as a diminution of God. 'Σὲ θεὸν ποιήσας' ('having made you God') repeats the deification of item 13. Not verified: the exact sense of 'πτωχεύει' in Hippolytus's other works.
